title: Why can every service look healthy (green health checks, normal CPU, low error rate) while the product is actually broken, and why do you need end-to-end business metrics and synthetic journeys (order-completion rate, payment-success rate) rather than only per-service dashboards?
shortTitle: Why all services can be green while the product is broken: business metrics and synthetic journeys
keyPoints: Per-service signals (readiness probes, CPU, 5xx rate) only say each part is individually alive, not that the composed flow works.
Failures in the seams: a flipped feature flag, bad data, or a silent logical error causes no crash but breaks the product.
Business-outcome metrics (payment-success rate, order-completion rate) measure the result the customer cares about.
Alert on the ratio of completions to initiations and on sudden drops to catch composition-level failures.
Synthetic journeys run a real end-to-end flow continuously against production, catching seam failures even during quiet hours.
Per-service probes localize the fault after a business metric says there is one: they are complementary, not a replacement.
Tag synthetic traffic so it never pollutes real business metrics.

s1_definition.oneliner: Green services mean the parts are alive; a green business metric means the product actually works: and only the second one tells you the customer is okay.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Per-service signals** – liveness/readiness probes, CPU, memory, HTTP 5xx rate. These tell you each individual service is running.
- **Seam failures** – bad data, a flipped feature flag, or a silent logical error causes no crash in any service but breaks the composed business flow.
- **Business-outcome metrics** – payment-success rate, order-completion rate. Measured at the outcome boundary, not inside one service.
- **Synthetic journeys** – an automated client that continuously executes a real end-to-end flow against production, asserting the business outcome.
- **Complementary layers** – business metric says 'product is broken,' synthetic journey says 'where in the flow,' per-service dashboards and traces say 'why.'
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India's branch where every department reports 'we are open and staffed.' The teller counter is green, the vault is green, the signature-verification desk is green. Yet Rajesh cannot complete a transfer, because the form passed between departments has the wrong field filled in. Every department is 'healthy,' but the customer walked out without his transfer. A synthetic journey is like sending a secret shopper through the whole process every minute and raising an alarm the moment the end-to-end transfer fails.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Three layers of observability:

  Layer 1: Business Outcome Metrics
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ transfers.initiated: 1523               │
  │ transfers.completed: 0    <- ALERT      │
  │ "Is the customer okay?"  -> NO          │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Layer 2: Synthetic Journeys
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Every 60s: create test transfer         │
  │ Assert: reaches COMPLETED in 30s        │
  │ Result: FAILED at step 3 (settlement)   │
  │ "Where in the flow?" -> Settlement step │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Layer 3: Per-Service Dashboards + Traces
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Payment Service: 200 OK, 0% errors      │
  │ Settlement Service: 200 OK, 0% errors   │
  │ Trace: settlement flag = OFF            │
  │ "Why?" -> Feature flag accidentally off │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Every service can be green while the product is broken because per-service signals and business outcomes measure completely different things. A readiness probe only answers whether one Pod can accept traffic. A low 5xx rate only means the service is not throwing server errors. None of these say whether the composed end-to-end flow that Rajesh cares about actually succeeds. The failures that slip through live in the seams: a flipped feature flag, bad data passed downstream, or a silent logical error.

The fix is to measure the outcome, not just the parts. Business-outcome metrics like transfer-completion rate alert when the ratio drops, even though every per-service dashboard is green. Synthetic journeys run a real end-to-end flow every minute, catching seam failures even during quiet hours when real traffic is too sparse for statistical significance.

At National Bank of India, Pankaj deployed a change with a settlement flag accidentally turned off. All weekend every dashboard was green, but no transfer completed. After adding a payment-completion-rate SLO and a synthetic journey, the next composition-level fault was caught within a minute.

Remember one sentence: green services only prove the parts are alive, so always add business-outcome metrics and synthetic journeys that measure what the customer actually experiences.
